extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics and research mathematicians (especially those interested in structuralism, category theory, and foundations)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and explaining the practical standards and methodological criteria mathematicians use when employing structural (category-theoretic/functorial) methods in definitions, proofs, and exposition; contrasts these with set-theoretic foundational demands. Targets how to practice and assess structural mathematics in research and textbooks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods must handle structures at every level
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods must handle structures at every level from natural numbers to functors by comparable means that readily relate any two levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These methods are used in practice, by necessity, with deductive rigor, even if they violate some philosophical theories. They should provide comparable ways of treating low-level objects (e.g. numbers) and high-level objects (e.g. functors) so that different levels are readily related in proofs and constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set-theoretic details must be rigorously irrelevant to theorems
rubrics_metrics.description: A set theoretic specification may be used in some step of a proof but those details must be rigorously irrelevant to the statement of the theorem (see discussion of Theorem 4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When textbooks or papers invoke set-theoretic constructions, they must ensure those 'nuts and bolts' do not affect the content of theorems; foundational choices should be confined to points (typically existence proofs) where they matter, and otherwise theorems and proofs should be formulated so that such details are irrelevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stipulation/tradition determines identity across structures
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no definition of identity preserving. Mathematicians stipulate which injections are identity preserving only taking care never to stipulate two distinct identity-preserving injections between the same patterns. Nearly everyone takes R↣C as identity preserving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners routinely 'identify' elements of one structure with elements of another (e.g. identify x with x+0i). Such identifications are conventional/stipulated (textbook practice), not dictated by set-theoretic logic. Conventions must avoid ambiguity (e.g. avoid stipulating two distinct identity-preserving injections between the same patterns).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer structural definitions up to isomorphism (universal-characterization style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fact 1 (characterization of R[X]) gives a rigorous definition of R[X] up to isomorphism which Lang does like to use; nothing in Fact 1 specifies the elements of R[X] as sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define objects by their position in patterns (e.g. universal properties, existence/uniqueness of morphisms) rather than by nuts-and-bolts set membership. Such characterizations are what mathematicians use in practice and are adequate for almost all reasoning; they capture the object 'up to isomorphism'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use morphism-based notion of isomorphism (category-theoretic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophers usually define an isomorphism of structured sets as a one-to-one onto function preserving structure; mathematicians today use a simpler and more general definition speaking of morphisms: a morphism f : S1 → S2 is an isomorphism if it has an inverse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt the morphism/inverse definition of isomorphism (suitable for categories) because it generalizes Bourbaki's set-based notion and better fits structural practice and higher-level categorical reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolate foundational dependence to few proofs (existence proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Structural practice isolates foundations in a few proofs, namely existence proofs as for Theorem 4. Definitions, theorems, and the great majority of proofs proceed rigorously without ever specifying the elements of any set at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, carry out definitions and arguments purely structurally; confine explicit set-theoretic element-specification to existence proofs or where foundations truly matter. This keeps most mathematics independent of particular foundational schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose foundations that support structural proofs when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs in ZF cannot all be structural because the axioms are not structural. Proofs in categorical set theory are entirely structural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that the choice of foundational framework affects whether proofs can be fully structural. If the goal is wholly structural development, categorical set theory better supports that aim; with ZF some proofs ultimately require elementwise specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize maps/morphisms over single structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Single structures matter less than the maps or morphisms between them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on relations and morphisms as primary objects of study; many results and unifications arise from functorial or morphism-level viewpoints rather than from isolated study of individual structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand maps and structures by embedding in higher-level patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Maps and structures are often best understood by placing them in higher level structures: 'Patterns themselves are positionalized by being identified with positions of another pattern'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use categorical/higher-level frameworks (categories of categories, functor categories, etc.) to conceptualize and relate structures and maps; this often makes previously unstatable results precise and transferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept and use morphisms that are not plain functions when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: In other important categories the morphisms are not functions but the useful pattern-theoretic properties still hold for them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be open to morphisms that are richer or different from set-theoretic functions; treat them as arrows in patterns whose properties (composition, identity, inverses) are the focus, rather than insisting on elementwise function interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek structural characterizations that unify and enable transfer
rubrics_metrics.description: The Fact, when it was found by Eilenberg and Steenrod (1945), turned out to characterize homology (up to isomorphism) as a pattern of functors ... This characterization enabled massive progress in homology. It also suggested useful variants such as K-theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for axiomatic or structural characterizations (facts/axioms that determine an invariant up to isomorphism) because they both explain existing multiplicity of definitions and enable generalizations and new constructions across areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer tools that are specific, practicable, and daily tested for rigor
rubrics_metrics.description: The tools used in textbooks and research are more specific than most philosophical proposals and are daily tested for rigor in principle and feasibility in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt methods and tools that have concrete mathematical implementation and that have been repeatedly vetted in actual proofs and constructions; philosophical generalities should be constrained by what works in mathematical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use structural methods to connect intuition/purity to rigor
rubrics_metrics.description: Structuralist tools give the most direct known path from 'pure' content to rigor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the aim is to elucidate intuitive or 'pure' mathematical content while ensuring formal rigor, structural tools (functors, categories, universal properties) are often the most direct route.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance intuition, purity, and practicality in method choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Intuition develops as knowledge does. Pure proofs are meant to be desirable for their own sake, as being more intrinsic to their subjects...Mathematicians eliminate homology from specific theorems only when they have an easier alternative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value purity and intuitive conceptual clarity, but choose methods on grounds of feasibility and insight: prefer pure/conceptual proofs when they provide genuinely new understanding; otherwise use more utilitarian techniques if they make proofs feasible and comprehensible to practitioners.
